domains.name: Strategy & Value
domains.summary: Sets out what the organisation wants from AI and how that serves its wider strategy: the ambition, the boundaries, the funding, the expected value and the roadmap. The aim is adoption driven by the organisation's own objectives, with choices made deliberately and revisited as technology, rules and expectations change.

controls.title: AI ambition aligned to organisational strategy
controls.objective: The organisation has a stated ambition for AI that is derived from its own strategy and objectives, and that leaders and staff can describe.
controls.rationale: AI adopted for its own sake produces scattered pilots that do not add up to anything the organisation needs. Tying the ambition to existing objectives gives every later decision on funding, priority and risk a test to apply: does this help us do what we are here to do.

levels.1: No stated ambition; AI activity is driven by individual interest or supplier offers.
levels.2: An ambition or vision statement exists, but it is generic, not linked to organisational objectives, or not agreed by leadership.
levels.3: An approved AI ambition, owned by a named person and expressed in terms of the organisation's objectives, is known across the organisation.
levels.4: Progress against the ambition is measured and reported, and AI activity that does not serve it is identified and challenged.
levels.5: The ambition is refined from evidence of what AI has delivered and from changes in the organisation's strategy.

criteria.text: An approved AI ambition states what AI is for in terms of the organisation's objectives.
The AI ambition has a named owner.
The AI ambition has been communicated across the organisation.

questions: What is the organisation trying to achieve with AI, and which organisational objectives does that serve?
Who approved the ambition, and where is it written down?
Can you show a recent AI decision that was tested against the ambition?
evidence: The approved AI ambition or strategy, showing links to organisational objectives
Approval record from the board or executive committee
Decision papers that refer to the ambition

steps: List the organisation's current strategic objectives and, for each one, write down where AI could help and where it has no part to play.
Draft a short ambition of one page that says what AI is for in terms of those objectives, not in terms of technology.
Name a senior owner for the ambition and get it approved by leadership through the normal decision route.
Communicate the approved ambition to all staff through existing channels and include it in AI induction material (see CUL-02 and PPL-01).
pitfalls: Writing a vision about the technology that could belong to any organisation and gives no test for choosing between proposals.
Getting approval but never telling staff, so the ambition exists only in a board paper.
artefacts: One-page AI ambition statement linked to organisational objectives
Objective to AI opportunity mapping table
Staff briefing note on the AI ambition

controls.title: Where AI will and will not be used
controls.objective: The organisation has decided, and recorded with reasons, the areas of its work where AI is encouraged, where it is allowed only under conditions, and where it is ruled out.
controls.rationale: Staff and suppliers need to know where effort is welcome and where it is not, before they invest time in a proposal. Stating the reasons lets people apply the boundaries to cases the list does not name, and lets the organisation revisit them when the reasons change.

levels.1: No stated boundaries; whether AI is suitable for an area is argued case by case, if at all.
levels.2: Some areas are informally favoured or avoided, but this is not written down, not reasoned, or not agreed by leadership.
levels.3: Approved strategic boundaries say where AI is encouraged, conditional or ruled out and why, fit the risk appetite and the policy, and keep some decisions with people.
levels.4: Proposals and live uses are checked against the boundaries, and pressure on them (repeated requests in a ruled-out area, for example) is reported and considered.
levels.5: Boundaries are adjusted from evidence such as outcomes, incidents and external change, and the reasons for each change are published internally.

criteria.text: Approved strategic boundaries set out the areas where AI is encouraged, allowed only under conditions, or ruled out, with the reason for each.
The strategic boundaries are consistent with the approved AI risk appetite (RSK-01).
The AI policy (GOV-01) reflects the strategic boundaries.
The strategic boundaries name the kinds of decision that must always be taken by a person.

questions: Which areas of your work are you actively seeking to use AI in, and which have you ruled out?
What reasons are recorded for the areas that are ruled out or conditional?
How do the boundaries show up in the AI policy and in how proposals are judged?
evidence: The approved statement of strategic boundaries, with reasons
Cross-references between the boundaries, the risk appetite and the AI policy

steps: Work through the organisation's main areas of work and sort each into encouraged, conditional or ruled out for AI, writing the reason for each choice.
Check each boundary against the approved risk appetite (RSK-01) and adjust any that would accept more risk than it allows.
List the kinds of decision that must always be taken by a person, such as those with serious effects on someone's rights or livelihood.
Get the boundaries approved and make sure the AI policy (GOV-01) reflects them, including the decisions reserved for people.
pitfalls: Recording the categories without the reasons, so nobody can apply them to a new case.
Setting boundaries that contradict the risk appetite or the policy, leaving staff unsure which applies.
artefacts: AI boundaries table with encouraged, conditional and ruled-out areas and reasons
List of decisions reserved for people

controls.title: Investment and funding for AI
controls.objective: The organisation has a defined approach to funding AI, covering what is paid for centrally and locally, how long commitments last, and how requests for money are judged.
controls.rationale: AI needs some shared spending (platforms, skills, governance) that no single team will fund, and much of its value only appears after more than one budget year. Without a funding approach, promising work stops when a pilot budget runs out, and money goes to whoever asks first rather than to what serves the ambition.

levels.1: AI is funded from whatever local budgets teams can find; there is no view of total spend.
levels.2: Some central or ring-fenced funding exists, but the rules for accessing it are unclear, it is year to year only, or it covers pilots and not running costs.
levels.3: A documented approach to funding AI sets central and local responsibilities, longer commitments where needed and published criteria, and is followed across the organisation.
levels.4: Total AI spend is known and reported against the funding approach, and funded work is reviewed against what it was funded to deliver.
levels.5: Funding allocation is adjusted from evidence of which investments delivered value, and the approach is refined each planning cycle.

criteria.text: A documented funding approach sets out which AI costs are the responsibility of central budgets and which of local budgets.
The funding approach provides multi-year commitments where the work needs them.
Criteria for judging requests for AI funding are published.
Funding decisions across the organisation follow the documented approach.

questions: How is AI work funded, and what is paid for centrally versus by individual teams?
Can work that proves itself in a pilot get funding to run and scale beyond the current year?
How are competing requests for AI funding judged, and by whom?
evidence: The documented funding approach or investment framework for AI
Budget papers showing AI allocations, including any multi-year commitments
Records of recent funding decisions against the stated criteria

steps: Decide which AI costs are paid centrally (for example shared platforms, licences and governance) and which are paid by individual teams.
Identify which AI commitments need funding over more than one year, such as platforms, contracts and skills, and agree how they are protected.
Write and publish the criteria used to judge funding requests, linked to the value case (STR-04) and prioritisation criteria (POR-02).
Document the funding approach, get it approved by finance and leadership, and apply it to every AI funding request from then on.
pitfalls: Funding AI only through one-year pilot budgets, so successful uses have no money to run once the pilot ends.
Publishing criteria but letting requests bypass them through local budgets.
artefacts: AI funding approach note setting out central and local responsibilities
Published funding request criteria and scoring sheet

controls.title: Organisation-level value case
controls.objective: The organisation has stated the value it expects from AI across its work, by type of value, with the assumptions behind each estimate written down.
controls.rationale: An organisation-level value case lets leaders judge whether the overall investment is worth making and which kinds of value to pursue first. Writing the assumptions down means they can be tested later, so the case improves rather than becoming a figure nobody can check.

levels.1: No organisation-level view of expected value; benefits are claimed use by use, if at all.
levels.2: Expected value is described in general terms, without estimates, assumptions or a split by type of value.
levels.3: An approved, owned value case states the gains expected from AI and the assumptions behind them, and is used in strategy and funding decisions.
levels.4: The value case is compared with tracked benefits from live uses, and assumptions that prove wrong are reported and corrected.
levels.5: The value case is refined each cycle from measured outcomes, and its accuracy over time is itself tracked.

criteria.text: An approved value case sets out the efficiency, quality, service and capability gains expected from AI.
The value case states the assumptions behind the expected gains.
The value case has a named owner.
Strategy and funding decisions refer to the value case.

questions: What value does the organisation expect from AI overall, and of what kinds?
What assumptions sit behind those estimates, and who owns them?
When did you last check the value case against what live uses have actually delivered?
evidence: The organisation-level value case, with assumptions recorded
Strategy or funding papers that draw on it
A comparison of the value case with tracked benefits

steps: Estimate the value expected from AI under four headings: efficiency, quality, service and capability.
Write down the assumptions behind each estimate, including what the comparison is and how confident the estimate is.
Name an owner for the value case and get it approved alongside the AI ambition (STR-01).
Use the value case when making strategy and funding decisions (STR-03), and set up tracking of whether benefits arrive through MON-03.
pitfalls: Counting only time saved and ignoring quality, service and capability gains.
Leaving assumptions unstated, so estimates cannot be challenged or checked later.
artefacts: Organisation-level AI value case with assumptions log
Value type definitions for efficiency, quality, service and capability

controls.title: Horizon scanning and external expectations
controls.objective: The organisation tracks changes in AI technology, regulation, peer practice and public expectation, and feeds what it finds into its AI strategy.
controls.rationale: AI capability, rules and public attitudes are changing faster than most planning cycles. An organisation that does not look outward will find its strategy overtaken, or will learn of a new obligation or a better approach from someone else.

levels.1: No organised scanning; individuals follow developments informally and share them ad hoc.
levels.2: Some scanning happens, for example a newsletter or occasional briefing, but it is not linked to strategy decisions.
levels.3: An owned horizon scanning activity covers technology, regulation, peers and public expectation, produces regular output and informs strategy decisions.
levels.4: Findings are logged with the action taken on each, and the time from a relevant external change to a strategy response is tracked.
levels.5: Scanning anticipates change well enough that the organisation acts ahead of it, and the scanning sources and method are reviewed against how useful they proved.

criteria.text: A defined horizon scanning activity covers AI technology, regulation, peer practice and public expectation.
The scanning activity has a named owner.
The scanning activity produces output on a regular cycle.
Scanning findings are considered in strategy decisions.

questions: How does the organisation keep track of changes in AI technology, regulation and practice elsewhere?
Who receives the findings, and can you show a strategy decision that one of them changed?
How do you find out how the people you serve feel about AI being used?
evidence: Horizon scanning outputs, such as briefings or a log of developments
Records showing findings were considered by the forum or in strategy papers

steps: Name an owner for horizon scanning and agree the four areas it covers: technology, regulation, peer practice and public expectation.
Choose a small set of sources for each area and set a regular cycle, such as quarterly, for reviewing them.
Produce a short regular summary of what has changed and what it could mean for the organisation.
Put each summary on the agenda of the forum or person that makes AI strategy decisions and record what was decided (see STR-08).
pitfalls: Collecting news without saying what it means for the organisation.
Scanning only technology and missing changes in regulation or public expectation.
artefacts: Horizon scanning source list by area

controls.title: Multi-year AI roadmap tied to planning
controls.objective: The organisation has a phased AI roadmap that is linked to its business and financial planning cycles and shows the points where it will decide whether to proceed.
controls.rationale: A strategy without a roadmap is hard to fund and hard to hold anyone to. Linking the roadmap to normal planning cycles means AI work competes for resources in the same process as everything else, and explicit decision points stop the organisation drifting into large commitments without choosing to.

levels.1: No roadmap; AI work is planned project by project, if at all.
levels.2: A roadmap exists but is a list of projects, is not linked to business or financial planning, or has no decision points.
levels.3: An approved, owned multi-year roadmap follows the planning cycles, sets decision points with criteria and names the capacity planned uses depend on.
levels.4: Progress against the roadmap is reported, decisions at each point are recorded with their evidence, and slippage is acted on.
levels.5: The roadmap is revised each planning cycle from delivery evidence, value achieved and external change.

criteria.text: An approved, phased AI roadmap covers several years.
The roadmap is aligned with the organisation's business and financial planning cycles.
The roadmap names its decision points and the criteria for each.
The roadmap has a named owner.
The roadmap names the capability, data and technology capacity, including compute and storage, that planned uses depend on, and shows which uses depend on which.

questions: Is there a roadmap for AI, and how far ahead does it look?
How does it connect to the organisation's business plan and budget cycle?
What are the next decision points, and what will each decision be based on?
evidence: The approved roadmap, with phases and decision points
Business or financial planning documents that reference it
Records of decisions taken at roadmap decision points

steps: Set out the planned AI work in phases over several years, aligned to the organisation's business and financial planning cycles.
Name the decision points in the roadmap and the criteria for deciding whether to proceed, change course or stop at each.
For each phase, list the capability, data and technology capacity (including compute and storage) that the planned uses depend on, and the dependencies between them.
Name an owner for the roadmap and get it approved through the same route as business plans and budgets.
pitfalls: Producing a list of projects with dates but no decision points, so the roadmap is never questioned.
Planning uses without the data, skills and compute they depend on.
artefacts: Phased AI roadmap with decision points and criteria
Dependency register for capability, data and technology capacity

controls.title: Stakeholder input to strategy
controls.objective: Staff, their representatives, service users, partners and, where relevant, the public and regulators have a real opportunity to shape the AI strategy, and the organisation can show what changed as a result.
controls.rationale: The people who do the work and the people affected by it see risks and opportunities that leaders do not. Involving them early produces a better strategy and makes it more likely to be accepted, while consultation after decisions are made does neither.

levels.1: The strategy is written by a small group without wider input.
levels.2: Some groups are consulted, but late, selectively, or with no record of what they said or what changed.
levels.3: A planned engagement approach involves the relevant stakeholder groups before the strategy is settled and records what they said and how the organisation responded.
levels.4: The reach and influence of engagement are measured, gaps in who has been heard are identified, and stakeholders are told what changed because of them.
levels.5: Stakeholder involvement is a continuing part of how the strategy is developed, and the approach is improved from participants' feedback.

criteria.text: A planned engagement approach identifies the stakeholder groups relevant to the AI strategy.
The identified groups are involved before the strategy is settled.
A record shows the input from each group and the organisation's response to it.

questions: Who was involved in shaping the AI strategy, and at what stage?
Which groups affected by your use of AI have not been heard?
Can you point to something in the strategy that changed because of stakeholder input?
evidence: The stakeholder engagement plan for the strategy
A record of input received and how the strategy responded

steps: Identify the stakeholder groups that should shape the AI strategy, such as staff, their representatives, service users, partners and, where relevant, the public and regulators.
Plan how and when each group will be involved, making sure it happens before the strategy is settled.
Run the engagement and record what each group said.
Record how the strategy responded to each main point, including where input was not taken up and why, and share that response with the groups (see CUL-03).
pitfalls: Consulting on a strategy that is already decided, so input cannot change anything.
Recording what people said but not what was done about it.
artefacts: Stakeholder engagement plan for the AI strategy

controls.title: Strategy review cycle
controls.objective: The AI strategy is reviewed on a set cycle and whenever defined triggers occur, and each change is recorded with its reason.
controls.rationale: A strategy written for one state of the technology and the rules will be wrong within a year or two. A fixed cycle keeps it current, defined triggers catch changes that cannot wait, and a change record lets people see why direction shifted.

levels.1: The strategy is not reviewed once written, or is rewritten only when leadership changes.
levels.2: Reviews happen, but irregularly, without defined triggers, or without a record of what changed and why.
levels.3: The AI strategy is reviewed by its owner on a set cycle and when defined triggers occur, and each change is recorded with its reason.
levels.4: Reviews draw on measured evidence such as value achieved, risk and incident trends and horizon scanning, and actions from each review are tracked to completion.
levels.5: The review cycle and triggers are themselves adjusted from experience, so the strategy is updated at the pace the organisation needs.

criteria.text: The AI strategy has a set review cycle.
Defined triggers, such as major regulatory, technology or organisational change, prompt a review outside the cycle.
Each review is carried out by the strategy's owner.
Changes to the strategy are recorded with their reasons.

questions: When was the AI strategy last reviewed, and when is the next review due?
What events would cause an unscheduled review?
What changed at the last review, and why?
evidence: Strategy version history or change log, with reasons
Papers and minutes from the most recent review

steps: Set a review cycle for the AI strategy, such as yearly, aligned to business planning.
Define the triggers that require a review outside the cycle, such as major regulatory, technology or organisational change, and link them to horizon scanning (STR-05).
Make the strategy owner responsible for carrying out each review and reporting the result to leadership.
Keep a change log that records each change to the strategy with its reason and date.
pitfalls: Setting triggers that nobody watches for, so only the yearly review ever happens.
Changing the strategy without recording why, so later readers cannot follow its history.

domains.name: Governance & Accountability
domains.summary: Sets out who is accountable for AI, how decisions about AI are made and recorded, and how the organisation keeps sight of the AI it uses. Governance here should be proportionate: light enough that low-risk use is not slowed, firm enough that high-risk use cannot happen without the right people deciding.

controls.title: AI policy
controls.objective: The organisation has an approved AI policy that states which uses of AI are permitted, which need approval and which are not allowed, and keeps it current.
controls.rationale: Without a policy, staff either avoid AI entirely or use it without guardrails. A clear policy is the first thing people look for and the basis every other control refers to.

levels.1: No organisation-wide policy; individual teams or staff set their own rules.
levels.2: A policy or guidance note exists but is incomplete, unapproved, or not widely known.
levels.3: An approved, owned and controlled AI policy sets the scope of AI governance and which uses are permitted, need approval or are prohibited, and all staff know it.
levels.4: Policy awareness and compliance are measured; the policy is reviewed on schedule and after significant incidents or external change.
levels.5: The policy is refined from evidence of how AI is actually used, incidents and lessons, and stays ahead of external change rather than reacting to it.

criteria.text: An approved AI policy states which parts of the organisation, uses and systems AI governance covers.
The policy states which uses of AI are permitted, which need approval and which are prohibited.
The policy's prohibited uses include the practices that the law bans.
The policy has a named owner and a review date.
The policy has been communicated to all staff.
The policy and its supporting governance documents are approved, version-controlled and retained.
Acceptable use terms are set for users of AI services the organisation offers to others, and are reviewed.
Breaches of the acceptable use terms by users of the organisation's AI services are acted on.

questions: Is there an AI policy approved at the right level, and when was it last reviewed?
Does it distinguish uses that are permitted, need approval, and are not allowed?

Communication or training records showing staff were told about it

steps: Write a policy that states what AI governance covers (which parts of the organisation, which uses and which systems) and sorts uses into permitted, approval-required and prohibited, with practices banned by law listed as prohibited.

Letting supporting documents drift out of version control so nobody knows which is current.

controls.title: Executive accountability
controls.objective: A named senior executive is accountable for the organisation's use of AI, with a defined remit, and reports on it to the board or equivalent.
controls.rationale: AI cuts across technology, data, risk and the business. Without one accountable executive it falls between functions, decisions stall and nobody owns the outcome.

levels.1: No one is accountable; AI is treated as a technology matter or left to enthusiasts.
levels.2: Someone is informally seen as the lead, but the remit is unclear or lacks authority.
levels.3: A named senior executive is formally accountable for AI under a written remit and reports on AI to the board or equivalent as a standing item.
levels.4: The board receives regular, evidence-based reporting on AI benefits, risks and performance, and challenges it.
levels.5: Accountability arrangements are reviewed against outcomes and adjusted as AI use grows or changes in nature.

criteria.text: A named senior executive is formally accountable for the organisation's use of AI.

Splitting accountability between several executives so nobody owns the whole picture.

controls.title: Decision rights proportionate to risk
controls.objective: Decision rights for approving, changing and retiring uses of AI are defined, scaled to risk, and followed.
controls.rationale: If every use needs the same approval, low-risk use is choked and people work around the process. If none does, high-risk use goes ahead unseen. Tiered decision rights give speed where it is safe and scrutiny where it matters.

levels.1: No defined approval route; uses of AI start wherever someone decides to try them.

controls.objective: The organisation has approved rules for reviewing and disclosing AI-generated content that it releases or relies on, so people know when AI was used.
controls.rationale: Content produced by AI can be wrong or misleading, and can be mistaken for the work of a person. Reviewing it before it is released or relied on, and saying plainly where AI was used, protects the people who meet it and keeps official records trustworthy.

levels.5: The appetite is recalibrated from evidence of outcomes, incidents and external change, and the board reviews whether it is enabling the intended use of AI.

controls.title: AI risk assessment method

controls.rationale: Different teams assessing AI risk in different ways produce results that cannot be compared or added up. A single method, built into the existing risk process, lets the organisation see its overall AI risk and makes sure the risks particular to AI are not missed.

controls.title: Impact assessment before deployment
controls.objective: Before a use of AI goes live, its likely effects on people and groups (including equality, privacy, rights and safety) and on society and the environment are assessed to a depth that matches its risk, and the findings are acted on.
controls.rationale: Risk assessment looks at the risk to the organisation; impact assessment looks at what the use of AI could do to the people it touches. Some harms, such as a group being treated less favourably, only appear when someone asks that question directly and before the system is in use.

levels.1: Effects on people are not assessed before go-live, or only after a complaint.
levels.2: Some impact assessment happens, for example for data protection, but equality, rights and safety are not covered consistently, or findings are not acted on.
levels.3: A proportionate impact assessment covering people, workforce, society and environment is signed off before each in-scope use goes live, kept current, and its mitigations tracked.
levels.4: Completion and quality of impact assessments are checked, assessments are revisited after significant change, and actual effects in live use are compared with what was predicted.
levels.5: Impact assessment shapes design from the start, and the method is improved from evidence of effects it missed.

controls.rationale: Putting a person in the loop does not help if they lack the time, information or authority to disagree with the system. Oversight has to be designed for each use so that human control is real where it is needed and not imposed as a formality where it adds nothing.

levels.1: Oversight is not designed; whether anyone checks AI outputs depends on the individual.
levels.2: Some uses have a human review step, but its purpose, timing and authority are not defined, or reviewers lack the information to challenge outputs.
levels.3: Every use of AI has a documented, risk-based oversight model with trained reviewers, tested before go-live to show they can detect problems and intervene.
levels.4: Oversight is checked in practice, for example override rates and review times, and signs of rubber-stamping or overload are acted on.
levels.5: Oversight designs are refined from evidence of where human review adds value and where it does not.

criteria.text: For every use of AI, a documented oversight model, set according to risk, states who reviews, when, with what information, and their authority to override or stop the use.

pitfalls: Naming a reviewer who lacks the time, information or authority to intervene.
Assuming oversight works without testing whether reviewers actually catch errors.

controls.title: Explanation and challenge for affected people
controls.objective: People affected by decisions that AI supports can find out that AI was involved, get an explanation they can understand, and challenge the outcome through a route that can change it.
controls.rationale: People are entitled to understand decisions made about them, and some have legal rights to do so. A working route to explanation and challenge also corrects individual errors and shows the organisation where a system is going wrong.

levels.1: Affected people are not told AI was involved and have no specific route to question the outcome.
levels.2: Explanations or challenge are available for some uses, or on request only, and the route may not be able to change outcomes.
levels.3: People know when AI is involved in decisions about them or in their interactions, can get a meaningful explanation, and can challenge outcomes through human review.
levels.4: Requests for explanation and challenges are logged, outcomes and response times are measured, and patterns are fed back to the owners of the use.
levels.5: Explanation and challenge are designed in from the start, and the route is improved from the experience of the people who use it.

controls.title: Risk of AI from suppliers
controls.objective: Before AI in a bought product or service is used, and when it changes, the organisation assesses what it does, how it uses data, how the supplier changes the model, and what assurance the supplier offers.
controls.rationale: Much of an organisation's AI arrives inside products it has bought, often switched on by a supplier update. The organisation carries the risk of that AI even though it did not build it, so it needs to understand it as well as it would its own.

levels.1: AI in bought products is not identified or assessed; it is accepted as part of the product.
levels.2: Some suppliers are asked about AI, but questions are ad hoc, cover only new purchases, or miss updates that add AI to existing products.
levels.3: Standard due diligence covers AI in new and existing bought products before use and at intervals, feeds each risk assessment, and keeps unregistered high-risk AI out.
levels.4: Gaps in supplier assurance are tracked to closure and reported, and reassessment results inform renewal and purchasing decisions.
levels.5: Due diligence is refined from incidents and supplier experience, and the organisation's requirements shape what suppliers offer.

domains.name: Portfolio & Use Cases
domains.summary: Covers how ideas for using AI are collected, ranked, tested and either scaled, stopped or retired. Treating uses of AI as a portfolio means effort goes to the uses most likely to pay off, weak ideas are stopped early and cheaply, and what works in one place is reused elsewhere.

controls.title: Idea intake open to all staff
controls.objective: Anyone in the organisation can propose a use of AI through a simple, well-known route, and every proposal is acknowledged and considered.
controls.rationale: Many of the most useful ideas come from the people doing the work, not from a central team. Without an open route, ideas are lost, pursued quietly outside governance, or only come from those who already know the right people.

levels.1: No route for proposals; ideas progress only if someone senior or technical takes them up.
levels.2: A route exists in some teams or functions, or is not widely known, and proposals are not always answered.
levels.3: A single, documented and owned intake route is open to all staff and publicised, and every proposal is acknowledged and logged in the pipeline register.
levels.4: Volumes, sources and response times are measured, and parts of the organisation that submit little are followed up.
levels.5: The intake route is refined from proposer feedback and conversion rates, and actively draws in ideas from under-represented groups and functions.

controls.title: Agreed prioritisation criteria
controls.objective: Proposed uses of AI are ranked against published criteria covering value, feasibility, risk, cost and strategic fit, applied the same way to every proposal.
controls.rationale: Demand for AI work usually exceeds the capacity to deliver it. Published criteria make choices explainable, stop the loudest voice winning, and keep the portfolio aligned with what the organisation is trying to achieve.

levels.2: Criteria exist but are informal, unpublished, or applied differently by different teams.

levels.4: Consistency of scoring is checked, and the realised value and cost of chosen uses are compared with their scores to test the criteria.
levels.5: Criteria and weightings are adjusted from portfolio outcomes and changes in strategy, and the effect of each change is reviewed.

controls.title: Pipeline register of proposed uses
controls.objective: A single register records every proposed and in-flight use of AI with its status, owner and decision history, and hands each entry to the AI inventory when it goes live.
controls.rationale: Without a register, leaders cannot see what is being explored, duplicate work starts in different places, and decisions are hard to trace. A clean hand-over to the AI inventory (GOV-06) means nothing goes live without being recorded.

levels.1: No register; proposed and in-flight work is known only to the people doing it.
levels.2: Lists are kept by individual teams or for some uses, with inconsistent fields and no decision history.
levels.3: A single maintained register records every proposed and in-flight use with its status, owner, stage and decisions, and hands live uses to the inventory.
levels.4: Register completeness and accuracy are checked, stalled entries are flagged and resolved, and register data is reported to the oversight forum.
levels.5: The register is used to manage the portfolio as a whole, informing capacity, funding and reuse decisions, and its design is improved from use.

controls.title: Stage gates from idea to retirement
controls.objective: Each use of AI passes through defined stages (explore, pilot, scale, operate, retire), with entry and exit criteria checked at each gate.
controls.rationale: Gates give a consistent point to ask whether a use should continue, and they let effort and scrutiny grow as the use grows. Without them, pilots drift into live service without the checks that live service needs.

levels.2: Stages are described but criteria are vague or optional, or gates are used only for some uses.
levels.3: Documented, risk-proportionate stages with entry and exit criteria apply to every use, with gate decisions and a running design record kept.
levels.4: Gate outcomes and time spent at each stage are measured, and uses that skip or stall at a gate are identified and dealt with.
levels.5: Gate criteria and stages are refined from evidence of which checks catch problems and which only add delay.

controls.title: Proportionate business case
controls.objective: Each use of AI has a business case scaled to its size and risk that states expected benefits, full costs and assumptions, and is approved before significant commitment.
controls.rationale: A business case forces the question of whether AI is the right answer and gives a baseline to judge the use against later. Making it proportionate stops small, low-risk uses being held up by paperwork meant for large investments.

levels.1: Uses go ahead without a stated case; benefits are assumed rather than described.
levels.2: Business cases are written for some uses, often large ones, but costs or benefits are incomplete or not quantified.
levels.3: Every use of AI has a plain-language business case, scaled by a template to its size and risk, covering problem, benefits, costs, assumptions and options, approved at a gate.
levels.4: Business case assumptions are revisited at later gates, and cases that no longer hold lead to a recorded decision to continue, change or stop.
levels.5: Estimates are calibrated against actual costs and benefits from past uses, so cases become more accurate over time.

controls.title: Safe experimentation
controls.objective: Staff can try AI quickly within defined guardrails covering approved environments, data limits, time limits and exit criteria.
controls.rationale: People learn what AI can do by trying it, and blocking all experiments pushes them towards unapproved tools. Clear guardrails make fast trials possible while keeping sensitive data and live services out of reach until a use has been properly assessed.

levels.1: No sanctioned route to experiment; trials happen informally, often with unapproved tools or real data.
levels.2: Some teams have a place or permission to experiment, but rules on data, duration and exit are unclear or inconsistent.
levels.3: A documented experimentation route with approved environments, data rules, time limits and exit criteria is open to all teams and used.
levels.4: Experiments are logged and checked against the guardrails, breaches are acted on, and the route's speed and take-up are measured.
levels.5: Guardrails and environments are adjusted from what experiments reveal, so the route stays fast and safe as tools and needs change.

controls.title: Pilot to production decisions
controls.objective: Every pilot ends in a recorded decision to scale, extend or stop, made against criteria and evidence agreed before the pilot started.
controls.rationale: Pilots that are never formally ended either drift into live use without proper checks or linger and absorb effort. Agreeing success criteria in advance stops results being judged by enthusiasm after the event.

levels.1: Pilots continue or end by default; decisions are not recorded.
levels.2: Some pilots have success criteria, but they are set late, loosely defined, or not used to decide.
levels.3: Every pilot has success and stop criteria agreed at the start and ends in a recorded, evidence-based decision to scale, extend or stop.
levels.4: Pilot outcomes are tracked across the portfolio, extensions are time-limited and reviewed, and pilots running past their end date are flagged and resolved.
levels.5: Decision criteria and pilot design are improved from how scaled uses perform in live service.

controls.title: Reuse across the organisation
controls.objective: Successful patterns, components and lessons from uses of AI are recorded so others can find them, and are reused before anything new is built.
controls.rationale: Different teams often face the same problem. Reuse cuts cost and time, spreads approaches already assessed and approved, and avoids several slightly different solutions that each need supporting.

levels.1: Each team starts from scratch; reuse happens only through personal contacts.
levels.2: Some patterns or components are shared, but there is no place to find them and no expectation to look.
levels.3: Reusable patterns, components and lessons are recorded in a known place, checked before new work starts, and each shared component has an owner.
levels.4: The amount of reuse and the effort it saves are measured, and proposals that duplicate existing work are caught at intake or the first gate.
levels.5: Assets are designed for reuse from the start, and the reuse library is curated and improved from how it is used.

controls.title: Retiring uses of AI
controls.objective: Uses of AI that no longer earn their place are withdrawn through a planned process that covers users, dependent processes and disposal or retention of models and data.
controls.rationale: AI that stays in use after it stops delivering costs money, carries risk and may give worse results as conditions change. Unplanned withdrawal leaves users stranded and leaves models and data behind with nobody accountable for them.

levels.1: Uses are left running or switched off without a plan; models and data are left in place.
levels.2: Some uses are retired deliberately, but steps for users, data and models are worked out each time.
levels.3: A documented retirement process, triggered by periodic review, withdraws uses of AI with care for users, people, data, models and hardware, and updates the inventory.
levels.4: Live uses are routinely reviewed against retirement triggers, retirements are checked for completion, and leftover models or data are found and dealt with.
levels.5: Retirement is planned from the design stage, and the process is refined from lessons of past withdrawals.

domains.name: Operating Model & Delivery
domains.summary: Covers who builds, buys, runs and supports AI, how sourcing choices are made, how running costs and suppliers are managed, and the standards delivery teams work to. A clear operating model lets AI move from pilot to dependable service without every team inventing its own way of working.

controls.title: Target operating model for AI
controls.objective: The organisation has a defined, approved operating model that states who builds, buys, runs and supports AI, and what is done centrally and what locally.
controls.rationale: Without an agreed model, central teams and business units duplicate effort, compete for the same scarce skills, or each assume the other is responsible. Whether the model is central, devolved or hub-and-spoke matters less than everyone knowing which it is.

levels.1: No defined model; AI work is done wherever capability and interest happen to exist.
levels.2: A model is described or emerging, but responsibilities between central and local teams are unclear or not followed.
levels.3: An approved operating model sets out who builds, buys, runs and supports AI, centrally and locally, through named and resourced teams, and is followed across the organisation.
levels.4: The model's performance is measured, for example delivery times, capacity and demand, and work done outside it is identified and addressed.
levels.5: The model is reviewed against outcomes and adjusted as AI use grows or its nature changes.

criteria.text: An approved operating model for AI is documented.
The model states which parts of building, buying, running and supporting AI are done centrally and which locally.
Each of these activities has a named responsible team with the resources to carry it out.
The interfaces between central and local teams are defined.
AI work across the organisation follows the model.

questions: Which teams build, buy, run and support AI, and where is that written down?

controls.title: Build, buy or configure approach
controls.objective: A consistent, documented method decides for each use of AI whether to configure tools already owned, procure, build, or wait, and the reasons are recorded.
controls.rationale: AI capability is increasingly built into products the organisation already pays for, so building or buying something new is often unnecessary. A consistent method weighs cost, speed, control, skills and lock-in, and avoids choices driven by habit or by whichever supplier asked first.

levels.1: Sourcing choices are made case by case, usually by whoever starts the work.
levels.2: Some guidance exists, but it is not used consistently or does not consider configuring existing tools or waiting.
levels.3: A documented sourcing method with set criteria decides whether to configure, procure, build or wait for every use of AI, and each decision is recorded.
levels.4: Sourcing decisions are reviewed against actual cost, delivery time and supportability, and departures from the method are explained and approved.
levels.5: The method's criteria are updated from the outcomes of past decisions and changes in the market.

controls.title: AI-aware procurement and contracts
controls.objective: Contracts for AI products and services set clear terms on data rights, intellectual property, notice of model changes, transparency and exit.
controls.rationale: Standard technology contracts often say nothing about how a supplier may use the organisation's data, who owns outputs, or what happens when the underlying model changes. Settling these terms at procurement is far easier than trying to add them once the service is in use.

levels.1: AI is bought on standard terms with no AI-specific clauses.
levels.2: AI-specific terms are added for some contracts, depending on who runs the procurement.
levels.3: Standard AI contract terms, informed by the supplier risk assessment, are used in every relevant procurement and cover rights, change, transparency, security, assurance, resilience, exit and liability.
levels.4: Contracts are checked for the standard terms before signature, departures are approved and recorded, and existing contracts are reviewed when renewed.
levels.5: Standard terms are updated from supplier disputes, incidents, market practice and legal change.

controls.title: Delivery standards for AI
controls.objective: AI work is delivered by multidisciplinary teams using user-centred methods to defined delivery standards.
controls.rationale: AI that works technically can still fail in use if it does not fit how people work. Teams that bring together users, business, data, technical and risk knowledge, and that test with real users as they go, are more likely to build something people adopt.

levels.5: Delivery standards are improved from user outcomes and lessons across the portfolio.

controls.title: Service management for live AI
controls.objective: Every live AI service has defined support, change and problem management arrangements, including handling of changes to models and prompts.
controls.rationale: Once live, AI needs the same support as any other service, plus extra care because its behaviour can change when models, prompts or data change. Without service management, problems go unreported and changes reach users untested.

levels.2: Some services are in the support process, but AI-specific changes such as model or prompt updates are not covered.
levels.3: Every live AI service has a support owner, a problem reporting route for users, and change and problem management that covers AI-specific changes.
levels.4: Service levels, problems and changes are measured and reported, and repeat problems lead to root cause fixes.
levels.5: Service management practice for AI is refined from incident and change data and from user feedback.

controls.title: Collaboration and sharing
controls.objective: The organisation works with peer organisations and partners to share AI solutions, lessons and capacity where this serves its aims.
controls.rationale: Many organisations face the same AI problems. Sharing solutions and lessons reduces cost and repeated mistakes, and pooled capacity gives smaller organisations access to skills they could not hold alone.

levels.1: No deliberate collaboration; contact with peers happens through individuals.
levels.2: Some collaboration or sharing takes place, but it is opportunistic and not tracked.
levels.3: A stated approach guides collaboration with peers and partners, and solutions and lessons are shared and taken up under agreed data, intellectual property and ethical terms.
levels.4: The value of collaboration is assessed, for example time or cost saved, and partnerships that do not deliver are changed or ended.
levels.5: Collaboration shapes the organisation's AI plans, and it contributes to and learns from shared work as a matter of course.

controls.title: Continuity when AI fails
controls.objective: Services that depend on AI can continue safely when the AI is unavailable, degraded or producing wrong results, through planned fallbacks that have been tested.
controls.rationale: AI services fail in ways other systems do not, including supplier outages, model changes and confident but wrong output. Services that rely on AI need a planned way to carry on, or to stop safely, so that a failure does not become harm to the people they serve.

levels.1: Dependence on AI is not considered in continuity planning; a failure would be handled when it happened.
levels.2: Some services have fallbacks, but they are informal, untested or do not cover degraded or wrong output.
levels.3: Every service that depends on AI has a tested fallback or safe stop, based on an impact analysis and part of continuity plans, and people are told when it is used.
levels.4: Recovery times are measured against targets, and failures in testing are fixed.
levels.5: Continuity is improved from tests, incidents and supplier changes, and the degree of dependence on AI is set deliberately for each service.

criteria.text: An impact analysis of AI unavailability exists for each service that depends on AI and sets its recovery objectives.

pitfalls: Planning only for outages and not for the AI giving confident but wrong answers.
Assuming staff can return to the manual process when the skills or capacity to do so have gone.

controls.title: Involving people in AI design and evaluation
controls.objective: Evaluations and research that involve people have their informed consent, ethics review and protection, use participants who represent those the service will serve, and for significant uses draw on the communities affected.
controls.rationale: Testing AI with people gives the best evidence of how it will work in use, but it puts those people at some risk and is only useful if they reflect the people the service will serve. Engaging affected communities early on significant uses brings concerns to light while the design can still change.

levels.1: Research and evaluation with people happen informally, without consent records or ethics review.
levels.2: Some projects obtain consent or ethics review, but there is no common standard, participants are chosen for convenience, or affected communities are not engaged.
levels.3: Evaluations and research involving people have informed consent, ethics review, representative participants and protection of wellbeing and the right to withdraw, and significant uses engage affected communities at planning and design.
levels.4: Consent, ethics review and participant representation are checked at delivery gates, and community input and the response to it are reviewed for significant uses.
levels.5: Research practice and community engagement are improved from participant feedback, outcomes and lessons across the portfolio.

criteria.text: Evaluations and user research involving people have the informed consent of participants.

domains.name: Data & Information
domains.summary: Covers the data and information that AI uses and produces: who owns it, whether it is good enough for the job, whether its use is lawful and fair, whether people can find and understand it, how long it is kept, who can reach it and where it came from. Most problems with AI in use trace back to data, so these controls apply to bought and embedded AI as much as to anything built in-house.

controls.title: Data strategy supports AI
controls.objective: The organisation's data strategy states what its planned uses of AI need from data and sets out how those needs will be met.
controls.rationale: AI ambitions often assume data that does not exist, cannot be joined up or is not allowed to be used. Writing AI's needs into the data strategy brings those gaps into view early, and lets data investment be planned alongside AI investment rather than after it.

levels.1: No data strategy, or one that does not mention AI; data needs are discovered project by project.
levels.2: The data strategy mentions AI in general terms, but does not state what data AI needs or how gaps will be closed.
levels.3: An approved, owned data strategy sets out what planned AI needs from data and the actions and funding to meet it, backed by an approved data architecture.
levels.4: Progress against the data actions that AI depends on is measured and reported, and slippage that puts AI plans at risk is escalated.
levels.5: The data strategy and the AI strategy are revised together, using evidence of which data constraints have most limited AI value.

criteria.text: An approved data strategy exists with an owner and a review date.
The strategy sets out what planned uses of AI need from data.
The strategy sets out the actions and funding to meet those needs.
An approved data architecture covers how data used by AI is taken in, stored, organised and maintained.

questions: Does the data strategy say what your planned uses of AI need from data?

steps: Gather what the planned uses of AI need from data, drawing on the AI strategy (STR-01) and roadmap (STR-06).

pitfalls: Writing the data strategy in general terms without naming the AI uses it serves.
Agreeing actions with no funding attached.

controls.title: Data ownership and stewardship
controls.objective: Every data set used by AI has a named accountable owner and day-to-day stewards who understand the data and look after it.
controls.rationale: Decisions about whether data can be used for AI, whether it is good enough and who may see it need someone with authority to make them. Without named owners and stewards these questions go unanswered, or are answered by whoever happens to be building the system.

levels.1: Ownership of data is unclear; system administrators or project teams make decisions about data by default.
levels.2: Some important data sets have named owners, but stewardship is informal and data used by AI is not consistently covered.
levels.3: Every data set used by AI has a named owner and steward, recorded centrally, with defined responsibilities for approving use, quality and access.
levels.4: Coverage of ownership and stewardship is measured, gaps are filled within a set time, and owners are held to their responsibilities through regular review.
levels.5: Owners and stewards actively shape how their data is used for AI, and the arrangements are improved from experience of where decisions were slow or missed.

criteria.text: Every data set used by AI has a named owner and a named steward.
Owners and stewards are recorded in a central record.
Owner and steward responsibilities for approving use, quality and access are defined.

controls.title: Data quality fit for purpose
controls.objective: The quality of data used by each AI system is assessed against what that use needs, and shortfalls are fixed or their effects managed before and during live use.
controls.rationale: AI reproduces the gaps, errors and skews in its data, often at scale and with confidence. Quality is relative to the use: data adequate for monthly reporting may be unfit for an automated decision about an individual.

levels.1: Data quality is assumed; problems are found when outputs look wrong.
levels.2: Quality is checked for some uses or some data sets, without agreed measures or a link to what the AI use needs.
levels.3: Quality requirements are set for each use of AI, data is assessed against them before and during use, and shortfalls are owned and remediated or mitigated.
levels.4: Quality measures are tracked over time for data used by AI, falls below threshold trigger action, and the effect of quality on AI outputs is understood.
levels.5: Quality issues are fixed at source, and requirements and checks are refined from evidence of which quality problems most affected AI outcomes.

criteria.text: Quality requirements, including relevance and representativeness for the intended purpose, are set for each use of AI.
Data is assessed against those requirements before use.

Each quality shortfall has an owner and a remediation or mitigation plan.

pitfalls: Checking completeness and accuracy but not whether the data represents the people or cases the AI will meet.
Assessing quality once before launch and never again.

controls.objective: Data available for AI is catalogued and described well enough that people can find it, understand what it means and its limits, and use it correctly.
controls.rationale: Teams that cannot find suitable data either give up or use the wrong data. Descriptions of meaning, coverage and known limits stop data being used for purposes it does not support, which is a common cause of misleading AI outputs.

levels.1: Knowledge of what data exists sits with individuals; finding data means asking around.
levels.2: Some data sets are listed or documented, but descriptions are incomplete, out of date or held in separate places.

levels.4: Catalogue completeness and accuracy are measured, and use of the catalogue is tracked to show whether people find what they need.
levels.5: Catalogue entries are kept current largely as a by-product of normal data work, and descriptions are improved from feedback by the people using them.

controls.title: Lawful and fair use of data
controls.objective: Before data is used in an AI system, its use is confirmed as lawful, consistent with the purpose for which it was collected, and fair to the people it describes.
controls.rationale: Using existing data for AI is often a new purpose that the original basis for holding it does not cover. Settling the lawful basis and fairness of each use before work starts avoids systems that have to be withdrawn, and protects the people whose data is used.

levels.1: Data is used for AI wherever it is available; lawful basis and fairness are not considered.
levels.2: Data protection advice is sought for some uses, usually late or only for obviously personal data.
levels.3: Each use of data in AI has a lawful basis, purpose check and fairness consideration signed off before use, with data minimised and privacy techniques considered.
levels.4: These records are checked for completeness against the AI inventory, are revisited when the use or the data changes, and gaps are acted on.
levels.5: Lawful and fair use is designed in from the start of each use of AI, and the approach is refined from case outcomes, complaints and changes in law.

controls.title: Records management for AI
controls.objective: Retention and records rules cover what AI systems take in and produce, including prompts, outputs and the decisions they supported, and are applied in practice.
controls.rationale: AI creates new kinds of information that may need to be kept as evidence of a decision, disclosed on request, or deleted on time. If records rules do not cover them, the organisation can neither explain past decisions nor show it is not keeping data longer than it should.

levels.1: No one has considered whether AI inputs and outputs are records; retention depends on product defaults.
levels.2: Some rules exist for some AI systems, but prompts, outputs and AI-supported decisions are not consistently covered.
levels.3: Records and retention rules cover AI inputs, prompts, outputs, supported decisions and system logs, and are applied to every use of AI.
levels.4: Application of the rules is checked, including retention settings in bought tools, and failures such as unretrievable records or late deletion are caught and fixed.
levels.5: Records handling for AI is largely automated, and the rules are refined from requests for information, audits and changes in how AI is used.

controls.title: Controlled access and sharing
controls.objective: AI systems and their users can reach only the data they need for the agreed purpose, and data is shared into and out of AI systems only under agreed rules.
controls.rationale: AI systems are often given broad access to make them work quickly, and then surface data to users who would never have been allowed to see it directly. levels.4: Access rights and sharing agreements for AI are reviewed on a set cycle, excess access is removed, and breaches of sharing rules are detected and acted on.
levels.5: Access and sharing controls for AI are applied automatically from data classification and purpose, and are refined from review findings.

controls.title: Provenance of training and test data
controls.objective: For data used to train, tune or test AI, the organisation knows and records where it came from, what rights it holds over it, and any limits on its use.
controls.rationale: Data of unknown origin can carry rights the organisation does not hold, biases nobody can trace, or restrictions that surface only after release. A recorded provenance lets these questions be answered, and lets a model be rebuilt or withdrawn if a source turns out to be unusable.

levels.1: Training and test data are gathered from wherever is convenient, and their origin is not recorded.
levels.2: Origin is recorded for some data sets, but rights, licences and limits are not consistently checked.
levels.3: For every data set used to train, tune or test AI, origin, rights, limits and preparation are recorded before use and linked to the models that used it.
levels.4: Provenance records are checked for completeness before release, and when a source's rights or limits change, affected models are identified and acted on.
levels.5: Provenance is captured automatically through data pipelines, and the approach is refined from audits, disputes and changes in rights or regulation.

domains.name: Technology & Platforms
domains.summary: Covers the technology through which AI is adopted: which tools and platforms people may use, how AI fits into the existing estate, where it is hosted, how models and prompts are tested, released and controlled, and how the organisation copes with fast change from suppliers. The aim is a small number of well understood routes that make the approved way the easy way.

controls.title: Approved AI tools and platforms
controls.objective: The organisation keeps a current list of approved AI tools and platforms, each with clear conditions of use, and staff know where to find it.
controls.rationale: Staff need a quick answer to which AI tools they can use and for what. An approved list with conditions turns policy into something people can act on, and gives procurement, security and data teams one place to record their decisions about each tool.

levels.1: No approved list; staff choose tools themselves or wait for case-by-case answers.
levels.2: Some tools are known to be allowed, but there is no maintained list, or conditions of use are missing or unclear.
levels.3: A maintained, published list of approved AI tools and platforms states each one's permitted uses, data limits and owner, with a route to request additions.
levels.4: The list is reviewed on a set cycle, requests are handled within an agreed time, and use of approved tools is measured against the conditions.
levels.5: The list is refined from usage, requests and supplier change, and approval of new tools is quick enough that staff rarely look elsewhere.

criteria.text: A maintained list of approved AI tools and platforms exists.
For each listed tool or platform, the list states its permitted uses, the data that may and may not be used with it, and its owner.

controls.title: Reference architecture for AI
controls.objective: Agreed architecture patterns set out how AI components fit into the technology estate, and new uses of AI follow them or record why not.
controls.rationale: Without shared patterns each team solves the same problems differently, which raises cost and leaves an estate that is hard to support or secure. A small set of agreed patterns speeds delivery and makes AI services easier to run and change.

levels.1: No agreed patterns; each use of AI is designed from scratch.
levels.2: Some patterns or preferred approaches exist, but they are informal, partial or not used consistently.
levels.3: Owned reference patterns cover the common uses of AI, are applied through design review, and build in explainability, traceability and guardrails proportionate to risk.
levels.4: Conformance with the patterns is checked and reported, and departures are tracked to see whether they show a pattern needs to change.
levels.5: Patterns are updated from delivery experience, operating data and technology change, and retired when better approaches arrive.

controls.title: Hosting and data location
controls.objective: Requirements for where AI is hosted and where its data is processed and stored are defined, and each use of AI is checked against them before and during live use.
controls.rationale: Many AI services process data in places the organisation has not chosen, sometimes in other jurisdictions or through subprocessors. Legal, contractual and sensitivity requirements on location only hold if they are stated and then checked against what the service actually does.

levels.1: Hosting and data location are not considered; they follow whatever the supplier offers.
levels.2: Location is checked for some services, usually at purchase, without stated requirements or later checks.
levels.3: Documented requirements set where AI may be hosted and data processed for each class of data, and every use, including subprocessors, is checked before go-live.
levels.4: Compliance with location requirements is rechecked on a set cycle and when suppliers change terms or infrastructure, and breaches are acted on.
levels.5: Location requirements are refined from changes in law, risk and the market, and checks rely on continuous supplier attestation rather than one-off reviews.

controls.title: Integration with existing systems
controls.objective: AI is connected to core systems through supported, documented interfaces that the organisation can maintain, change and switch off.
controls.rationale: AI is most useful when it works with the systems people already use, but informal connections break silently, are hard to change and can become critical without anyone noticing. Supported and documented integration keeps AI services maintainable and lets them be removed cleanly.

levels.1: AI is connected to other systems by whatever means works, often manual workarounds or unsupported links.
levels.2: Some integrations are documented and supported, but others are informal or known only to the people who built them.
levels.3: Every integration between AI and core systems is supported, documented and can be switched off safely, and AI permissions on other systems are limited and approved.
levels.4: Integration health and failures are tracked, undocumented integrations are found and brought under control, and changes go through managed change.
levels.5: Integration patterns are standardised and reused, and improved from incidents and change experience.

controls.title: Managing models in live use
controls.objective: Models, prompts and their configuration are versioned and released under control, so the organisation knows what is running and can roll back to a known good version.
controls.rationale: A small change to a model, prompt or setting can change behaviour as much as a code change, and suppliers may change models without notice. Version and release control means problems can be traced to a change and reversed quickly.

levels.1: Models and prompts are changed directly in live use; there is no record of what changed or when.
levels.2: Some versioning exists, for example for in-house models, but prompts, settings or supplier model versions are not controlled and rollback is uncertain.
levels.3: Models, prompts and configuration are versioned, released with approval and can be rolled back, with documentation for each version and advance notice of changes to users.
levels.4: Releases and rollbacks are recorded and reviewed, unplanned changes including supplier model updates are detected, and failed releases are investigated.
levels.5: Release and rollback are largely automated and routinely exercised, and the process is refined from release outcomes.

controls.title: Testing and evaluation before release
controls.objective: Before release, each AI system is tested for accuracy, robustness and behaviour against acceptance criteria agreed in advance, and released only if it meets them.
controls.rationale: AI can perform well in a demonstration and badly on real cases, unusual inputs or the groups it serves least well. Testing against criteria set before results are seen gives the release decision an objective basis and a record to compare live performance with.

levels.1: Systems are tried informally before release; there are no acceptance criteria.
levels.2: Some testing is done, but criteria are set after the fact, test data is unrepresentative, or robustness and behaviour are not covered.
levels.3: Every release is tested against criteria and operating conditions set in advance, on representative data, with results signed off and the approach reviewed against live performance.
levels.4: Test coverage and results are reviewed across uses, releases that miss criteria are blocked or formally accepted, and test results are compared with live performance.
levels.5: Test methods and criteria are refined from live performance and incidents, and evaluation is automated and repeated for every change.

Testing of generative AI covers harmful output.

controls.title: Technology change and refresh
controls.objective: The organisation plans for changes to models, suppliers and platforms, including suppliers withdrawing models, so that AI services continue without disruption.
controls.rationale: AI models and platforms are replaced and withdrawn far faster than most enterprise technology, often on the supplier's timetable. Planning for that change avoids services stopping or being kept on unsupported versions, and keeps the organisation able to move to better options.

levels.4: Dependency end dates and supplier notices are tracked across the estate, changes are scheduled ahead of deadlines, and services caught by unplanned change are reviewed.
levels.5: Services are designed so models and platforms can be swapped with little rework, and refresh planning is improved from experience of past changes.

controls.title: Unapproved AI tools

levels.4: The level of unapproved use is measured over time, repeat or high-risk use is escalated, and findings feed changes to the approved tools list.

domains.name: AI Security
domains.summary: Sets out what an organisation needs in place to adopt AI securely. This is a bridge domain: it asks whether the organisation has adopted a security baseline for AI, assesses AI-specific threats, manages the security of its AI supply chain, protects information, tests AI security before release and can respond to AI security incidents. levels.4: Conformance with the baseline is checked and reported for each use of AI, and gaps are tracked to closure or formally accepted.
levels.5: The baseline is updated from incidents, threat intelligence and changes in recognised frameworks, and the organisation contributes to shared practice.

levels.4: Leakage controls are monitored, attempted exposures are detected and followed up, and results are reported.
levels.5: Controls are refined from monitoring and incident data so that protection improves without adding friction for legitimate use.

controls.title: AI in security incident response
controls.objective: Security incident management covers incidents involving AI, with playbooks, people who have the skills to handle them, and the ability to contain an affected AI service quickly.
controls.rationale: An attack on or through an AI service can look different from a conventional incident and may need a model, tool or integration to be switched off fast. Preparing before an incident happens avoids slow, improvised responses. Non-security AI incidents are handled under MON-04.

levels.2: The incident process mentions AI, but there are no AI playbooks and few responders know how AI services work.
levels.3: Security incident procedures include exercised AI playbooks, trained responders and a known containment route for each AI service, with disclosure and notification routes set.
levels.4: Response performance is measured, and lessons from exercises and real incidents are acted on.
levels.5: Incident response for AI is improved from exercise results, real incidents and external threat information, and lessons are shared with peers.

controls.title: Security testing of AI before release
controls.objective: Before release, each AI system is security tested against the threats in its threat model by suitably skilled testers, including checks that it does not disclose personal or sensitive information.
controls.rationale: An AI system that passes its accuracy tests can still be manipulated, talked out of its safeguards or made to reveal information it holds. Testing against the threats found for the use, by people who know how AI is attacked, finds these weaknesses before an attacker does.

levels.1: Systems are released without security testing, or with conventional checks that miss AI-specific threats.
levels.2: Some security testing is done, but it is not driven by the threat model, testers lack AI skills, or safeguard bypass and information disclosure are not covered.
levels.3: Every release is security tested against its threat model by suitably skilled testers, independent for higher-risk uses, including safeguard bypass for generative AI and checks for disclosure of personal or sensitive information.
levels.4: Security test coverage and findings are reviewed across uses, and releases with unresolved findings are blocked or formally accepted.
levels.5: Security test methods are refined from incidents and live performance, and security testing is repeated for every change.

domains.name: People & Skills
domains.summary: Covers the knowledge and skills people need to use AI safely and well, from a baseline for everyone to specialist careers, and how the organisation plans for the effect of AI on its workforce. Capability should be built inside the organisation rather than rented, and changes to roles should be planned in the open with the people affected.

controls.title: AI literacy for all staff
controls.objective: Everyone in the organisation has a baseline understanding of what AI is, what it can and cannot do, and how to use it safely under the organisation's policy.
controls.rationale: Staff meet AI in the tools they already use, whether or not the organisation plans for it. A shared baseline lets people spot unreliable output, avoid sharing what they should not, and see where AI could help their work.

levels.1: No organisation-wide AI learning; understanding depends on individual interest.
levels.2: Some AI awareness material exists, but it is optional, reaches few staff or is out of date.
levels.3: Everyone who uses or operates AI for the organisation must complete a defined AI literacy baseline that is kept current, and completion is recorded.
levels.4: Completion and understanding are measured across the organisation, gaps by group are followed up, and content is refreshed on a set cycle.
levels.5: The baseline is updated from incidents, staff feedback and changes in AI tools, and its effect on safe use is assessed.

criteria.text: A defined AI literacy baseline covers what AI can do, its limits and its risks.
The baseline covers the AI policy, the adopted ethical principles, and the environmental and social impact of AI use.
The baseline covers the AI security threats relevant to all staff, and updates are issued as new threats appear.
The baseline is required for all staff, including new joiners.
The baseline is also required for contractors and others who operate AI on the organisation's behalf.
Completion of the baseline is recorded for everyone it is required of.

questions: What does every member of staff need to know about AI, and where is that set out?

steps: Write a short literacy baseline that covers what AI can and cannot do, its main risks, the security threats every member of staff could meet, the AI policy (GOV-01), the adopted ethical principles (RSK-05) and the environmental and social effects of AI use.

controls.title: Leadership capability
controls.objective: Leaders understand AI well enough to set direction for it, question proposals and risks, and make informed decisions about its use.
controls.rationale: Leaders approve AI investment, accept its risks and set the tone for how staff use it. If they cannot judge claims made for AI, decisions are left to enthusiasts or vendors, or are not taken at all.

levels.2: Some leaders have attended AI briefings, but there is no defined expectation of what leaders should know.

controls.title: Specialist roles and careers
controls.objective: The organisation defines the specialist AI roles it needs, with career paths and a professional community that help people grow and stay.
controls.rationale: Specialists who have no defined role or route to progress tend to leave or move into unrelated work. Clear roles and careers make it possible to recruit, develop and keep the people who build, assure and run AI.

controls.title: Workforce planning for AI
controls.objective: The expected effect of AI on roles, numbers and skills is planned for openly, with affected staff and their representatives informed and involved, and decisions made fairly.
controls.rationale: AI can change what roles involve, create new ones and reduce demand for some tasks. Planning this in the open, and treating redeployment, reskilling and growth as real options, keeps trust and avoids losing knowledge the organisation still needs.

levels.3: A known, resourced support route gives current guidance on every approved AI tool, including its limits and security risks, and tells users promptly of security changes.
levels.4: Use of support, common questions and response times are measured, and recurring problems feed changes to guidance, learning or tools.
levels.5: Support is shaped by how people actually use AI, and good practice from users is captured and shared back.

Tool guidance stating limitations, failure modes and residual risks

Agree a routine with the owners of each tool so guidance is updated whenever the tool changes.
Set up a way to tell users promptly about security-relevant changes, such as a short notice on the support page and a message to users.

Publishing guidance at launch and never updating it when the tool changes.
Describing only what a tool can do and leaving out where it fails.
