domains.name: Culture & Change
domains.summary: Covers the human side of adopting AI: managing it as organisational change, telling people plainly what is happening and why, involving staff and their representatives, making it safe to raise problems, and keeping the trust of the people the organisation serves. Technology that people do not trust or understand is either not used or used badly, so these controls decide whether the rest of the framework produces real benefit.

controls.title: Planned approach to AI change
controls.objective: AI adoption is managed as organisational change, with a change plan, named sponsors and the resources to carry it out.
controls.rationale: Most of the effort in adopting AI goes into changing how people work, not into the technology. Treating adoption as a technology rollout leaves processes, roles and habits unchanged, and the expected benefits do not arrive.

levels.1: No change approach; AI tools are made available and people are left to work out what to do with them.
levels.2: Some change activity happens on individual projects, but there is no organisation-wide plan or dedicated resource.
levels.3: A documented AI change plan, based on an assessment of the current culture, has named senior sponsors and funded resource, and is applied to every significant use.
levels.4: Progress against the change plan is measured and reported, and areas where adoption is stalling are identified and given extra support.
levels.5: The change approach is refined from what has and has not worked in earlier rollouts and from changes in the scale and type of AI being adopted.

criteria.text: An assessment of the current culture and what has to change for AI adoption has been carried out.
A documented change plan for AI adoption is in place and builds on that assessment.
The change plan has named senior sponsors.
A funded change resource is in place to carry out the plan.
The change plan is applied to every significant use of AI.

questions: Is there a change plan for AI adoption, and who sponsors it?
What people and budget are assigned to change, as opposed to delivery?
How is the change approach applied to a new use of AI going live?
evidence: The AI change plan, with sponsors, resources and timescales
Change plans or impact assessments for recent uses of AI

steps: Assess the current culture and how people work today, using a short survey and conversations with teams, and record what has to change for AI to be used well.
Write a change plan for AI adoption based on that assessment, with aims, activities and timescales.
Name senior sponsors and set aside a budget and people for change work, separate from delivery.
Make a change plan or a proportionate change section a requirement for every significant use of AI, checked at the stage gates (POR-04).
pitfalls: Treating AI adoption as a tool rollout and putting all the budget into technology.
Writing a plan without first finding out how people work and feel today.
Naming sponsors who have no time or authority to act.

Change section template for individual uses of AI

controls.title: Internal communication about AI
controls.objective: Staff receive clear, honest and regular communication about what AI is being used for, why, and what it means for them.
controls.rationale: In the absence of information, people assume the worst, usually that AI is being brought in to cut jobs. Open communication, including about limits and problems, builds the trust that adoption depends on.

levels.1: Communication about AI is occasional, comes from enthusiasts or suppliers, and is not coordinated.
levels.2: Announcements are made about some uses of AI, but they focus on benefits, are irregular or reach only some staff.
levels.3: An owned communication plan delivers regular, honest messages to all staff about AI use, purpose, limits and effect on staff.
levels.4: Reach and understanding are measured, for example through surveys, and messages are adjusted where staff are confused or concerned.
levels.5: Communication is two-way as a matter of course, and its content and channels are improved from staff feedback and observed understanding.

criteria.text: A communication plan for AI is in place and has an owner.
The plan sets out regular, honest messages about AI use, its purpose, its limits and its effect on staff.
The messages reach all staff.

questions: How do staff find out which uses of AI are planned or live, and why?
Does communication cover limits, problems and the effect on jobs, as well as benefits?
How do you know the messages have been understood?
evidence: The communication plan and a sample of recent messages

steps: Name an owner for internal communication about AI.
Write a communication plan that sets the channels and frequency, and commits to covering what AI is used for, why, its limits and its effect on staff.
Publish regular updates that include problems and limits as well as benefits, and keep a list of planned and live uses of AI that staff can see.
Check that the plan reaches all staff, including those without regular computer access or on leave.
pitfalls: Only announcing successes, which staff quickly stop believing.
Avoiding the question of jobs, which leaves people to assume the worst.
Leaving communication to suppliers or enthusiasts.
artefacts: Staff-facing list of planned and live uses of AI

controls.title: Staff and representative engagement
controls.objective: Staff and their representatives, including trade unions where present, are involved early in decisions about AI that affect their work, and their input is considered and answered.
controls.rationale: The people who do the work know where AI will help and where it will cause problems. Involving them and their representatives before decisions are made produces better uses of AI and avoids the resistance that follows when change is presented as already decided.

levels.1: Staff and representatives hear about AI after decisions are made, if at all.
levels.2: Engagement happens on some projects or late in the process, often as consultation on a decided plan.
levels.3: Affected staff and their representatives are involved at design stage of significant uses of AI through a defined route, their input is recorded, and they hear what changed.
levels.4: The timing and effect of engagement are tracked, and uses of AI that skipped it are identified and addressed.
levels.5: Staff and representatives help shape the AI agenda itself, and the engagement approach is improved from their feedback on how well it works.

criteria.text: A defined route is in place for engaging affected staff and their representatives on uses of AI.
Affected staff and their representatives are involved at the design stage of each significant use of AI.
Their input is recorded.
They are told what changed as a result of their input.

questions: At what point are affected staff involved in a proposed use of AI?

Agree with representative bodies, where they exist, how and when they will be involved.
Hold engagement sessions with affected staff and representatives during design and record what they said.
Report back to those involved what changed as a result of their input, and what did not and why.
pitfalls: Consulting on a plan that has already been decided.
Recording input but never telling people what happened to it.
Engaging only with managers and not with the staff who do the work.

controls.title: Safe to raise concerns
controls.objective: Anyone can raise a concern or report a problem with AI without fear of blame, and can see what was done about it.
controls.rationale: The first signs that AI is producing wrong or harmful results are usually noticed by the people using it. If they fear blame or expect nothing to happen, they stay quiet and the problem grows.

levels.1: There is no known route for raising AI concerns; problems are raised informally or not at all.
levels.2: A route exists, such as a general helpdesk or whistleblowing policy, but staff do not know it covers AI or doubt that it is safe to use.
levels.3: An owned, no-blame route for raising AI concerns is known to all staff, and everyone who raises a concern hears what was done.
levels.4: Use of the route and staff confidence in it are measured, and response times and outcomes are monitored and reported.
levels.5: Raising concerns is seen as normal practice, and the route and the response to it are improved from staff feedback and trends in what is raised.

criteria.text: A no-blame route for raising AI concerns is in place and has an owner.
The route has been communicated to all staff.
People who raise a concern receive a response on what was done.

questions: If a member of staff thought an AI tool was giving wrong or unfair results, what would they do?
How do you know staff feel safe to raise AI concerns?
What happens after a concern is raised, and does the person hear back?
evidence: Guidance describing the route for raising AI concerns
A log of concerns raised, with responses and outcomes
Staff survey results on confidence in speaking up

steps: Choose or set up a route for raising AI concerns, which can be an existing route explicitly extended to cover AI, and name its owner.
Write down that concerns raised in good faith will not lead to blame, and get senior leaders to say so publicly.
Tell all staff about the route, with examples of the kinds of AI concerns it is for.
Log each concern and give the person who raised it a response on what was done, with links to the incident process (MON-04) where needed.
pitfalls: Assuming staff know that a general whistleblowing policy covers AI.
Taking concerns in but never telling the person what happened.
Making the route anonymous only, so there is no way to reply.

controls.title: Learning from what did not work
controls.objective: Experiments and uses of AI that fail or are stopped are reviewed without blame, and the lessons are recorded and shared.
controls.rationale: Many AI experiments should not continue, and stopping them is a sign the process works. If stopped work is hidden or treated as failure, teams repeat the same mistakes and become unwilling to try things.

levels.1: Stopped or failed work is quietly dropped; lessons stay with the people involved.
levels.2: Some teams review what went wrong, but findings are not recorded or shared beyond the team.
levels.3: Every stopped or failed AI experiment or use has a no-blame review, and its lessons are recorded in a shared place and passed to relevant teams.
levels.4: Lessons are checked for take-up, for example in new proposals and stage gates, and repeat mistakes are identified and followed up.
levels.5: Lessons from inside and outside the organisation are used routinely to shape new proposals, and stopping work early is recognised as good practice.

criteria.text: A no-blame review is held for every stopped or failed AI experiment or use.
Lessons from each review are recorded in a shared place.
Lessons are communicated to the relevant teams.

questions: What happened to the last AI experiment that was stopped, and what was learned?
Where are lessons recorded, and who reads them?
How are teams who stop an experiment treated?
evidence: Review records for stopped or failed AI work
A lessons log or library, with evidence it is used in new proposals

steps: Set a short no-blame review format, focused on what happened and what to do differently, not on who was at fault.
Make the review a required step whenever an AI experiment or use is stopped or fails, linked to the stop decision (POR-07).
Record lessons in one shared place that anyone proposing AI can search.
Send each new lesson to the teams it is relevant to, for example through the community of practice (CUL-06).
pitfalls: Reviewing only failures and not work that was stopped for good reasons.
Writing long reports nobody reads instead of short, searchable lessons.
Letting reviews turn into blame, which makes teams hide problems next time.

controls.title: Champions and communities
controls.objective: Networks of champions and communities of practice, with time and support to do so, spread know-how about AI and good practice across the organisation.
controls.rationale: People learn most from colleagues doing similar work. A supported network of champions reaches parts of the organisation that central teams cannot, and brings practical problems back to the centre.

levels.1: A few enthusiasts help colleagues on their own initiative and in their own time.
levels.2: A champions network or community exists in some areas, but without agreed time, support or a link to the central AI team.
levels.3: A champions network with defined roles and agreed time covers all major business areas, and a centrally supported community of practice meets regularly.
levels.4: Champion coverage and activity are tracked, and the network's effect on adoption and good practice is measured and reported.
levels.5: The network shapes guidance, tools and priorities, and its structure is refreshed as adoption spreads and needs change.

criteria.text: A champions network covers all major business areas.
Champions have a defined role and agreed time for it.
A community of practice for AI meets regularly.
The community of practice receives central support.

How much time do champions have for the role, and who supports them?
How do issues raised by champions reach the people who can act on them?

steps: Write a champion role description that sets out what champions do and how much time they get, and agree that time with their managers.
Recruit champions so that every major business area has at least one.
Set up a community of practice that meets regularly, with a central contact who supports it and passes issues to the people who can act.
Keep a list of champions by area and a record of community meetings.
pitfalls: Asking champions to do the role on top of a full workload with no agreed time.
Concentrating champions in technical teams and leaving front-line areas uncovered.
Treating the network as a substitute for a resourced support route (PPL-08).

controls.title: Adoption support for affected teams
controls.objective: Teams whose work changes because of AI get practical support through the change, and actual adoption is tracked against what was planned.
controls.rationale: Going live is not the same as being used well. Teams need time, help and adjusted processes to change how they work, and without tracking nobody knows whether a tool is being used as intended, worked around or ignored.

levels.1: Teams are given the tool and expected to adapt; nobody checks whether it is used.
levels.2: Some teams get support at launch, but it stops soon after and adoption is not tracked.
levels.3: Every team affected by a significant use of AI has a support plan for the change, and adoption is tracked against planned levels.
levels.4: Adoption data is reviewed regularly, teams falling behind receive targeted support, and the reasons for low adoption are recorded and acted on.
levels.5: Support approaches are improved from adoption patterns across many rollouts, and new rollouts plan support from that evidence.

criteria.text: Every team affected by a significant use of AI has a support plan.
Each support plan covers process changes, time to adapt and help after go-live.
Adoption is tracked against planned levels.

questions: For a recent use of AI, what support did the affected team receive before and after go-live?
How do you know whether the team is actually using it as intended?
What happens when adoption is lower than planned?
evidence: Support plans for teams affected by recent rollouts
Adoption tracking data compared with planned levels

Track actual adoption against those levels after go-live and share the results with the team and its business owner.
pitfalls: Stopping support at launch week, when most adjustment happens later.
Measuring logins rather than whether the tool is used for the intended work.
Expecting teams to adapt without time set aside from their normal workload.

controls.title: Public and customer trust
controls.objective: The organisation understands how the people it serves view its use of AI and takes that into account in its decisions and how it explains itself.
controls.rationale: An organisation's use of AI can be lawful and still lose the confidence of the people it serves. Knowing their views and expectations early lets it avoid uses they would not accept and explain the ones they would.

levels.1: Public or customer views on the organisation's AI use are not sought; reaction is discovered only through complaints or media coverage.
levels.2: Views are gathered occasionally, for example on a single project, but are not used consistently in decisions.
levels.3: The views of the people the organisation serves on its AI use are gathered through a defined approach and shape design decisions and explanations.
levels.4: Levels of trust are measured over time, and changes in trust or emerging concerns lead to recorded action.
levels.5: The people served help shape decisions about where and how AI is used, and the approach to building trust is improved from measured results.

criteria.text: A defined approach is in place and used to gather the views of the people the organisation serves on its use of AI.

Use what you learn to shape how each use of AI is explained to the people it affects.

Gathering views and not recording how they affected any decision.
Asking only people who already support the use of AI.

domains.name: Measure & Improve
domains.summary: Covers what happens once AI is in use: setting measures before go-live, monitoring live behaviour, tracking whether benefits arrive, handling non-security incidents and notifying serious ones, independent assurance, listening to users, re-running this assessment and reporting to leadership. Without measurement the organisation cannot tell whether AI is working, causing harm or worth its cost.

controls.title: Performance measures and baselines
controls.objective: Each use of AI has agreed performance measures and a recorded baseline of current performance before it goes live.
controls.rationale: Without a baseline taken before go-live, nobody can show later whether AI made things better or worse. Agreeing measures in advance also stops success being defined after the event to fit whatever happened.

levels.1: Measures are not set; success is judged by impression or anecdote.
levels.2: Some uses of AI have measures, but they are set after go-live, lack a baseline or cover only technical performance.
levels.3: Every use of AI has owned measures of accuracy, outcome, effect on people and reliance, with baselines set before go-live and proxies for risks not yet measurable.
levels.4: Measures and baselines are checked at stage gates, and uses without them are stopped or held until they are in place.
levels.5: Measures are refined from experience of which ones actually predicted success or problems, and common measures allow comparison across uses.

criteria.text: Every use of AI has agreed measures covering accuracy, service outcome and effect on people, with a named owner.

Setting measures after go-live, when no baseline can be taken.

controls.title: Monitoring live AI
controls.objective: Live AI is monitored against its measures for accuracy, drift, misuse and unexpected behaviour, with thresholds that trigger action.
controls.rationale: AI that worked at go-live can degrade as data, users or the underlying model change, often without any visible failure. Continuous monitoring with set thresholds catches this before it causes harm.

levels.1: Live AI is not monitored; problems are found when users complain.
levels.2: Some uses are monitored, usually for availability or cost, without checks on output quality or thresholds for action.
levels.3: Every live use of AI is logged and monitored against thresholds, operating conditions, fairness measures and provider instructions, with named people to respond to breaches.
levels.4: Monitoring results are reviewed on a set cycle, threshold breaches are tracked to resolution, and monitoring coverage is itself checked.
levels.5: Monitoring methods and thresholds are tuned from incident history and changes in models and use, and early warning signs are acted on before thresholds are reached.

criteria.text: Every live use of AI is monitored for accuracy, drift, misuse and unexpected behaviour against defined thresholds.
Event logging is enabled for each use of AI while it is in use.

Each use is monitored against its defined operating conditions.
Each use is monitored against the fairness measures set under RSK-06.
Each use is monitored for personal or sensitive data appearing in its outputs.

pitfalls: Monitoring availability and cost only, with no check on the quality of outputs.

controls.title: Serious AI incidents and external notification
controls.objective: The organisation defines serious AI incidents, can suspend a use of AI when needed, and tells suppliers, regulators and affected people through set routes and within set deadlines.
controls.rationale: When AI causes or risks serious harm, the law may set short deadlines for telling the supplier and the regulator, and the people affected need to hear promptly. levels.2: Some notification duties are known, but serious incidents are not defined, deadlines are not set, or no one is named to suspend a use.
levels.3: Serious AI incidents are defined, notification routes and deadlines and a decision point to suspend use are set, affected people are told under a plan, and risks short of a serious incident are reported and acted on.
levels.4: Serious incidents lead to reviews of the use concerned, and notification and suspension decisions are reviewed with their actions tracked to completion.
levels.5: Lessons from serious incidents, including those reported by other organisations, routinely change designs, controls and notification arrangements.
